title: A story for a grieving king
hookLine: Yudhishthira asks if any king was ever more unlucky, and a sage begins the story of Nala and a golden swan
carry: hearing sacred stories is devotion too

cards: Has there ever been a king more unlucky than me? Yudhishthira asks it in the forest camp, with Arjuna gone and his brothers missing him. He's the one who threw the dice, and he can't stop going over it.
The question sounds like a complaint and is really a plea, and he puts it to a visiting sage named Brihadashva. The sage tells a story. There was a king, he says, who also lost his kingdom at dice.
His name was Nala. And the story begins, of all places, with a bird.

teach.b: Nala is king of the Nishadhas: handsome, truthful, and a master with horses.
Far away, in Vidarbha, lives Damayanti, daughter of King Bhima. The two have never met, but each keeps hearing about the other, and each begins to love someone they have never seen.

teach.h: A GOLDEN SWAN CARRIES THE NEWS.
teach.b: One day, in a garden, Nala catches a swan with wings that shine like gold. The swan speaks. Let me go, it says, and I'll praise you to Damayanti so well she'll think of no one else.
Nala lets it go. The swan flies to Vidarbha, and when Damayanti reaches for it, it speaks to her of Nala. Her answer is simple: say the same of me to him.
Then Damayanti grows pale and quiet, and her father decides it's time for her swayamvara, the ceremony where a princess chooses her own husband. Now step back and see why the sage tells this here.
Yudhishthira wants to know if his suffering is the worst there has ever been. The sage doesn't argue. He tells a sacred story and asks him to listen to the end.
That's a real Hindu practice: katha, telling and hearing sacred stories. In the Bhagavata Purana, Prahlada names nine ways of devotion, and the first is shravana, simply hearing.

teach.h: A STORY TO HOLD A GRIEF.
teach.b: It's why families still gather for a katha, and in the epic's own telling, whoever tells Nala's story need not fear the bad luck that hounded him. For today: when someone is hurting, you don't always need advice.
Listening to a sacred story together is devotion too.

how: The story of Nala and Damayanti is told within the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, by the sage Brihadashva to Yudhishthira, and Hindus still gather to hear sacred stories told aloud as katha.

games.q: Yudhishthira asks: was any king ever more unlucky than me? you're the sage. what do you do?
o: list his mistakes so he learns from them.
tell him a sacred story about another king who lost everything at dice, and ask him to listen to the end.
tell him to cheer up, others have it worse.
games.why: Brihadashva tells Nala's story. in Hindu devotion, hearing a sacred story, shravana, is itself a way to God.

practice: Bring to mind one sacred story you were told when you were small: Ganesha and the mango, Krishna stealing butter, Prahlada and the pillar, any at all, and the person who told it.
Remember how it felt to be handed it, and breathe with that memory. If you pray, remember that person in your prayer; if not, simply stay with being told a story.
